summary: Briefly describes packet satellite technology developed by DARPA and partners in the U.K. and Norway, and lists papers about its experience.

eli5.summary: A reading list about sending data packets through a satellite that many ground stations share.

subtitle: A bibliography of papers about DARPA's packet satellite network technology and experiments.

tldr.problem: Researchers working with packet satellite technology needed access to papers documenting the designs, experiments, and operational experience of SATNET and related systems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC is a bibliography describing the history of packet satellite technology—from the early ALOHA experiments at the University of Hawaii through DARPA's Atlantic Packet Satellite experiment (SATNET)—and lists key papers covering the technology's development.
tldr.outcome: The document provides a reference guide to the major technical publications about packet satellite networks, supporting ongoing research and experimental work.

today: RFC 829 is an informational reference document. Packet satellite technology as described here became a foundation for later experiments in satellite networking, though the specific systems mentioned (SATNET, MATNET) are no longer operational.

sections.title: The History of Packet Satellite Technology
sections.content:
Packet satellite technology grew out of early work on packet switching over multiaccess radio channels at the University of Hawaii, supported by DARPA. The key difference from the ARPANET was that the ALOHA system let many transmitters dynamically share a common radio channel, rather than using dedicated point-to-point circuits.

In the ALOHA system, many terminals shared a single transmit frequency, and a central receiver at the University of Hawaii acknowledged successful reception on a different frequency. Terminals retransmitted after a random delay if they did not receive an acknowledgement. This concept was later demonstrated to work over a satellite channel linking Hawaii and NASA-Ames via the ATS-1 satellite.
sections.eli5: A team in Hawaii made a way for many radios to share one channel by taking turns and trying again if they did not hear back. Later, they sent the same idea through a satellite.

sections.title: The Atlantic Packet Satellite Experiment (SATNET)
sections.content:
Starting in 1973, DARPA built an actual packet satellite system using an INTELSAT-IV satellite. The Atlantic Packet Satellite experiment (SATNET) was carried out with the British Post Office, COMSAT Corporation, Linkabit, and Bolt Beranek and Newman, later joined by the Norwegian Telecommunication Administration and the German Aeronautics and Space Research Establishment.

Between 1975 and 1978, SATNET underwent broad performance evaluations and tests. From 1979 onward, it served as a stable support for international experiments in command and control technology. The RFC also notes DARPA and the Naval Electronic Systems Command demonstrated a Mobile Access Terminal Network (MATNET) using packet satellite techniques over a FLTSATCOM satellite channel.
sections.eli5: DARPA built a real satellite system with help from partners in many countries. It worked for years running experiments, and it showed the idea could send both voice and data.

sections.title: The Bibliography
sections.content:
The RFC provides 31 numbered references covering the foundations of packet satellite technology, the design and operation of SATNET, and alternative techniques for shared-channel access. References cover early ALOHA work, the ARPANET's foundational papers, various channel assignment strategies, SATNET design and operation, and experimental results. Key authors include Jon Postel, Robert Kahn, Norman Abramson, and others who shaped early packet networking.

The papers span from 1970 to 1982 and cover theoretical analysis, system design, operational experience, and potential services for satellite networks. This collection forms the technical foundation for understanding how packet switching evolved to work over satellite links.
sections.eli5: The RFC lists 31 papers by the people who invented and tested these ideas. Reading them shows how the whole thing was built, step by step.
